interactive.title: The slope tracker over a top
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens with the slope tracker's linked graphs: two graphs, one above the other, sharing the same x across. The top graph shows an amount you want the most or the least of. A point P can be dragged along it, the tangent at P rides with it, and the bottom graph drops a dot at the same x, as high as the tangent's slope, which a readout also gives. First comes 40 m of barrier tape round a rectangular work area with one side x metres: one side and the next together take half the tape, so the other side is 20 − x, the area is A = 20x − x² square metres, and its slope is 20 − 2x. As P climbs to the top at x = 10, a 10 m square of 100 m², the slope readout falls to 0 and the dots cross the axis from plus to minus. The bottom line's own slope is the second derivative: −2 here, falling, which marks a top. On the cup-shaped example y = x² − 8x + 20 it is 2, rising, which marks a bottom, at x = 4. Then y = x³, which is flat at 0 but keeps climbing, so its slope dots touch the axis without crossing it. Then a source with an open-circuit voltage E and an internal resistance r feeding a load: the power into the load is the terminal voltage, E − Ir, times the current I, so P = EI − I²r. For an example 12 V source with 0.5 Ω inside, the top is at 12 A and 72 W, where the load is 0.5 Ω too. Then an open box folded from a 30 cm square sheet with squares of side x cut from its corners: the base is 30 − 2x each way, so its volume is V = x(30 − 2x)² = 4x³ − 120x² + 900x cubic centimetres, and the slope readout reads 0 at 5 cm, the largest box, 2,000 cm³, and again at 15 cm, where no base is left. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a flat-point puzzle shows only a short stretch of its curve near P until you check, and a wrong pick is shown going wrong on the graphs.
interactive.ignores: Every rule is an example, chosen so the numbers come out exactly; the 0.5 Ω and 3 Ω sources are picked for easy sums, not taken from a real battery. The tape has sharp corners and none spent on knots. The source keeps the same internal resistance at every current; a real battery's changes with its temperature and how charged it is. The box's sheet has no thickness and its folds take no material. The slope readout is worked from a very short chord, so it is rounded.

explain.text:
A smooth curve is flat for an instant wherever it turns over at a top or a bottom, so its derivative there is zero, and setting the derivative to zero finds the largest or smallest value. Here is why. Ride a point along a curve that climbs and then falls. While it climbs, the tangent slopes up and the slope is plus; once it falls, the tangent slopes down and the slope is minus. On a smooth curve the slope changes gradually, with no jumps, so on its way from plus to minus it passes through zero, and it does so just where climbing stops and falling starts: at the top. There the tangent is level, and the derivative is zero where a graph has a level tangent.[^1] A place where a curve turns like this is a [[turning point]], and at a turning point the derivative is zero.[^2] On the slope tracker you see it twice over: the slope readout passes through zero, and the dots on the bottom graph cross the axis, just as P rides over the top.

Take 40 m of barrier tape round a rectangular work area. If one side is x metres, two neighbouring sides take half the tape, 20 m, so the other side is 20 − x, and the area is A = x(20 − x) = 20x − x² square metres. A long thin strip encloses very little, so which shape encloses the most? The power rule gives dA/dx = 20 − 2x. Set it to zero: 20 − 2x = 0, so x = 10 m, the other side is 20 − 10 = 10 m too, and the area is 10 × 10 = 100 m², a square. Either side it is less: at x = 4 the area is 4 × 16 = 64 m² with slope 12, and at x = 16 it is 64 m² again with slope −12. To tell a top from a bottom without trying values, look at how the slope itself changes: its rate of change is the second derivative from the last lesson. Here d²A/dx² = −2, so the slope is falling, from plus through zero to minus, and the flat point is a top, the largest the area can be, its [[maximum]]. On a cup-shaped curve the slope rises from minus through zero to plus, the second derivative is plus, and the flat point is a bottom, its [[minimum]]. Engineering maths asks for exactly this: first and second derivatives give the position and the nature of a turning point.[^3]

A zero slope is a candidate, not a guarantee. Away from the ends, a top or a bottom of a smooth curve can only be where the slope is zero,[^4] but a zero slope need not be a top or a bottom.[^5] The curve y = x³ climbs, is level for an instant at x = 0, then climbs again: its slope, 3x², is 3 at x = −1, 0 at x = 0 and 3 at x = 1, plus on both sides. Its second derivative, 6x, is 0 there too, so that test cannot decide; look at the slope just either side instead. Two more limits keep the rule honest. A curve with a sharp corner, like the ridge of a roof, can turn over there without ever being flat, because its slope jumps straight from plus to minus. The capacitor's voltage in the last lesson had a corner too, where its slope jumped from climbing to 0, but there it held steady rather than turning over. And when x can only run between two ends, the largest value may sit at an end; if it is not at an end, it is at a turning point.[^6] So check the ends as well.

This is how engineers find the most of something. A source such as a battery has a resistance inside it, r. By Ohm's law a current I drops I × r across it, so the voltage at its terminals is its open-circuit voltage E less that drop, V = E − Ir. So the power into the load is P = VI = (E − Ir)I = EI − I²r. A small current carries little power, and a large current drops most of E across r, leaving little voltage at the terminals, so somewhere between, the power is largest. Take an example source with E = 12 V and r = 0.5 Ω: P = 12I − 0.5I², so dP/dI = 12 − I, which is zero at I = 12 A, where P = 144 − 72 = 72 W, against none at 0 A or at the short-circuit 24 A, and the second derivative, −1, says it is a top. With letters, E − 2rI = 0 gives I = E ÷ (2r), the terminal voltage falls to E ÷ 2, and so the load's resistance, V ÷ I, comes out equal to r: the most power reaches a load whose resistance matches the source's. Finding that condition by differentiating is a standard engineering problem.[^7] It is the most power, not the best use of it: at 12 A the source also turns 12² × 0.5 = 72 W into heat inside itself. This fixed r is a simplified picture, since a real source's internal resistance changes as it works. When the slope equation is too hard to solve, read it off the picture. Fold an open box from a 30 cm square sheet with squares of side x cut from its corners. Small cuts make a wide but shallow tray, big cuts a deep box on a small base, so the largest lies between: V = x(30 − 2x)² = 4x³ − 120x² + 900x, so dV/dx = 12x² − 240x + 900. The slope readout hits zero at x = 5 cm; check it by putting it back, 300 − 1200 + 900 = 0. The box holds 5 × 20 × 20 = 2,000 cm³, more than the 1,936 cm³ at 4 cm or the 1,944 cm³ at 6 cm. The slope is zero again at 15 cm, but that is a bottom, where no base is left. **Away from the ends, a top or a bottom of a smooth curve is where the derivative is zero,[^2] so set the derivative to zero to find it, then use the second derivative, or the slope just either side, to tell which it is.[^3]**

analogy.text: Picture an overhead cable sagging between two poles of the same height. From one pole it slopes down, then up again to the other, and at its lowest point, midway, it is level: a spirit level laid on it there would read level, and nowhere else on the span would. A graph's top or bottom works the same way: the place it sits level is where it turns.
analogy.breaks: Level does not always mean lowest: a cable laid over a flat ledge partway down a bank is level there and carries on downhill after it, like y = x³ at 0. And a sagging cable finds its lowest point by itself under gravity; on a graph nothing does, so you find it by setting the slope to zero.

practice.text:
- Write the amount you want the most or the least of as a rule in one thing you can choose. If a fixed amount ties two lengths together, like 40 m of tape, use it to write one in terms of the other.
- Differentiate term by term with the power rule.
- Set the derivative to zero and solve for the thing you choose. If the equation is too hard to solve, find where the slope changes sign by trying values, and close in on it.
- Tell a top from a bottom: a minus second derivative means a top, a plus one a bottom. If it is zero, look at the slope just either side.
- Check the ends of the range too, because the largest or smallest value can sit there.
- Put your answer back into the rule to get what was asked for, the area, power or volume, with its unit.

**Rules of thumb:** a top or bottom of a smooth curve is flat, but flat is not always a top or a bottom. The slope falling through zero means a top; rising through zero, a bottom.

**Safety:** work maximum power out on paper, never by trying loads on a real supply. At its top a source turns as much power into heat inside itself as it delivers, and a battery with a low internal resistance can drive a dangerous current.

**Worked example:** Say an example source has an open-circuit voltage of 9 V and an internal resistance of 3 Ω. The power into the load is P = 9I − 3I², so dP/dI = 9 − 6I. Set it to zero: 6I = 9, so I = 1.5 A. The second derivative is −6, so this is a top. The power there is 9 × 1.5 − 3 × 1.5² = 13.5 − 6.75 = 6.75 W. Check either side: at 1 A it is 9 − 3 = 6 W, and at 2 A it is 18 − 12 = 6 W, both less. The terminal voltage is 9 − 1.5 × 3 = 4.5 V, so the load is 4.5 ÷ 1.5 = 3 Ω, the same as the source's internal resistance.

**Common mistakes**
- Not bringing the power to the front: treating 3I² as giving 3I makes 9 − 3I = 0 and I = 3 A, where the load gets no power at all.
- Stopping at the x: the question asks for the area, power or volume, so put it back into the rule.
- Taking every zero slope for a top: y = x³ is flat at 0 and is neither.
- Forgetting the ends: on a range, the largest value can be at an end, where the slope need not be zero.

interactive.html:
Linked graphs sharing one x across: above, an amount you want the most or the least of; below, its slope at the same x.

Every rule is an example, and every dot below is the slope worked out from the rule above.

checks.label: The derivative is zero where the function has a horizontal tangent: wherever P sits where the slope is 0 (the tape at 10 m, the cup at 4, y = x³ at 0, the 12 V source at 12 A, the box at 5 cm and at 15 cm, and every puzzle's answer) the tangent drawn through P is level and P's dot below sits on the zero line; on the tape the dots run from plus, through 0 at the top, to minus

At the turning point of a curve the differential coefficient is zero: at every top or bottom here (the tape's 10 m, the cup's 4, 12x − 3x² at 2, the 12 V source's 12 A, the 24 V source's 4 A, the box's 5 cm, 2x² − 12x + 25 at 3, x³ − 12x at 2) the slope from the rule is 0, and the value there is higher than one grid step either side, or lower on both

First and second derivatives give the position and nature of a turning point: where the slope is 0, a minus second derivative goes with the slope falling from plus to minus, a top (tape −2, 12x − 3x² −6, the 12 V source −1, the 24 V source −6, the box −120), and a plus one with it rising from minus to plus, a bottom (the cup 2, 2x² − 12x + 25 4, x³ − 12x 12)

Local extrema can only occur at critical points: on every curve here, wherever the rule's value is higher, or lower, than at both neighbouring sample points, the slope passes through 0 between those neighbours (eight such places, none on y = x³ or x³ − 3x² + 3x)

Critical points are candidates for local extrema, not certainties: y = x³ at 0 and x³ − 3x² + 3x at 1 have slope 0 but are neither, their values rising through them with the slope plus on both sides; y = x³'s second derivative there is 0; and their slope dots touch the zero line without going below it

If an absolute extremum is not at an endpoint it is at an interior local extremum: over each range drawn, the largest box (2,000 cm³ at 5 cm), the most power (72 W at 12 A, 48 W at 4 A) and the largest area (100 m² at 10 m) sit inside, where the slope is 0, while the smallest, 0, sit at both ends

Differentiation finds the condition for the most power from a source to a load: for P = EI − I²r the slope is 0 at I = E ÷ (2r), 12 A for 12 V and 0.5 Ω and 4 A for 24 V and 3 Ω, where the load V ÷ I equals r (0.5 Ω, 3 Ω) and the power, 72 W and 48 W, is the most at any current; 40 W at 4 A and 20 A, 0 W at the short-circuit 24 A, and 12² × 0.5 = 72 W of heat inside
Every dot below is the rule's slope: on every screen each dot sits straight under its x, as high as the slope the chords there settle on from either side, and the tangent through P has that slope

From the rules, by hand: the tape at 4 m is 4 × 16 = 64 m² with slope 12, at 16 m slope −12, at 10 m 100 m²; the cup's slope is −4, 0, 4 at 2, 4, 6 and its bottom 4; 12x − 3x² is 12 at 2; y = x³ has slope 3, 0, 3 at −1, 0, 1; x³ − 3x² + 3x is 0, 1, 2 at 0, 1, 2 with slope 3, 0, 3; the 12 V source gives 72 W at 12 A, 40 W at 4 A and 20 A, 6 V and 0.5 Ω; the 24 V source 48 W at 4 A (96 W without 3I²), a 3 Ω load; the box 2,000 cm³ at 5 cm, 1,936 at 4, 1,944 at 6, slope 132 and −108 at 4 and 6, 0 at 15; 2x² − 12x + 25 is 7 at 3 and 25 at 0; x³ − 12x is −16 at 2, slope −9 and 15 at 1 and 3; and the screens' words quote these values

Every puzzle offers three different answers and accepts only the right one; each wrong answer is the slip it stands for: 0 m and 20 m against 10 m; a bottom and neither against a top; a top and a bottom against neither; 96 W and 0 W against 48 W; 4 cm and 15 cm against 5 cm; 3 and 25 against 7; a top and neither against a bottom

Before an answer no puzzle shows it: no tangent, no dot under P, nothing red, and the working ends in a question mark; a right answer shows the level tangent and P's dot on the zero line with nothing red, and every wrong answer shows its slip in red
Dragging P keeps it on its graph's grid inside the axes (whole metres and amps, half centimetres, half steps of x) and leaves a dot at every grid point it passes
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 1.3 s
